editorNote: From the flight line to the modem jack, home computing puts bigger choices on a smaller budget.
morningLine: A bomber crew needs a captain; software copyright reaches a Commons vote; new machines promise more for less.

lead.headline: Fifty Mission Crush puts the B-17 campaign on home computers
lead.dek: SSI trades arcade spectacle for the fortunes of a bomber crew in April’s simulation review.
body: A home-computer flight need not be a test of reflexes. Strategic Simulations’ Fifty Mission Crush makes the player responsible for an Eighth Air Force B-17 and the men aboard it. James V. Trunzo’s April COMPUTE! review finds its pull in a campaign of decisions and consequences rather than lavish graphics.

Operating from Britain, the crew flies against targets in Germany, France and the Netherlands. Fuel competes with bomb load; altitude, formation and cloud cover shape the prospects of a mission. Gunners must be assigned, and an abort can be wiser than pressing on with a damaged aircraft. Damage can even keep the bombs from leaving the bay.

The ambition is fifty missions, but individual sorties need not consume an evening. Trunzo reports flights as short as five minutes and seldom longer than fifteen, with the campaign saved after each mission. Menus and a concise booklet help make keyboard command approachable. The review calls the game challenging and addictive, while finding its graphics functional rather than spectacular.

Listed at $39.95, the simulation requires an Atari with at least 40K and BASIC, an Apple II-series machine with at least 48K, or a Commodore 64; all require a disk drive. This is an April review selection, not a claim that the game first reached shops this week.

stories.headline: Commons passes software-copyright bill at third reading
body: The House of Commons gave William Powell’s Copyright (Computer Software) Amendment Bill its third reading and passed it on April 19. The proposal would apply the Copyright Act 1956 to a computer program as to a literary work. Commons passage is a parliamentary step, not Royal Assent or final enactment.

Members debated commercial copying, search warrants and penalties as software became a larger business. John Butcher cited provisional computer-services turnover of £2,120 million in 1984, against £1,750 million in 1983. An estimate of nearly £150 million in annual piracy losses was an industry claim repeated in debate, not an independently audited total.

The Federation Against Software Theft’s case joined legal remedies to technical deterrents. As quoted by Andrew Hunter, its position acknowledged that no technical method alone would stop a determined thief, and warned against protection that imposed unacceptable costs or reduced value for legitimate users.

stories.headline: Atari promises a mouse-and-window computer for $599
body: Atari’s new price challenge fills the April magazine desk: an announced $599 520ST with 512K and an 8MHz Motorola 68000. Tom R. Halfhill’s COMPUTE! preview reports the January Winter CES promises, including a proposed 128K 130ST at $399. Those figures are computer prices, not complete monitor-and-drive packages.

Digital Research GEM brings icons, windows, drop-down menus and a two-button mouse. MIDI, serial and parallel interfaces suggest uses from music to printing, while the preview lists color and high-resolution monochrome display modes. Atari projected second-quarter availability; preproduction specifications and prices are promises, not evidence of retail delivery.

stories.headline: Commodore 128 promises three ways to preserve a software library
body: Commodore’s answer rests on keeping yesterday’s disks useful. April’s COMPUTE! preview describes three personalities: C64 compatibility, native 128K operation under the 8502, and Z80A operation with CP/M 3.0 loaded from disk. Native BASIC 7.0 and 40/80-column choices expand the machine’s working range.

The magazine tried SpeedScript 3.0 in C64 mode, but did not claim an exhaustive compatibility trial. A numeric keypad and dedicated Help, Escape, Tab and display keys mark a more work-oriented keyboard. April or May was a projected introduction window; an under-$300 indication was not an officially announced CES price.

market.headline: The modem price umbrella starts to leak
market.summary: Arlan R. Levitan’s April column links cheaper chip sets and consumer-brand competition to falling modem prices. Panasonic’s $99.95 300-bps KX-D401 and $299.95 1200-bps KX-D402 frame a market also courting Atari and Commodore owners at lower announced prices. These are period quoted prices, not a local stock check.

worldAnchor.headline: Discovery returns; NASA assesses heat-shield damage
worldAnchor.summary: Discovery landed at Kennedy on April 19 with Sen. Jake Garn and six crewmates. Tile loss damaged a wing flap and a tire burst after a brake locked; NASA was assessing possible schedule effects, not announcing a confirmed delay.

bbsNote.headline: Cheap modems and faster Delphi access
bbsNote.summary: April 1985 Levitan column covers January CES announcements and current service pricing; not an exact-week BBS event. Posts below are editorial source summaries, never purported surviving BBS messages.

posts.platform: Online Official Airlines Guide; service not named in anecdote
posts.text: Levitan recounts using a lap computer and acoustic cups at Detroit airport to find alternate flights after cancellation; the trip was to January CES, recounted in April.
Column reports 2400-bps access in 34 major cities at $5/hour extra, on top of $16/hour business or $6/hour nonprime service.
The Learning Phone cartridge announced at CES would provide PLATO access with high-resolution graphics; estimated cartridge price $30–$40, not confirmed retail availability.

curiosity.headline: A telephone with a modem inside
curiosity.summary: Panasonic’s KX-D4130 combines the desk phone and computer link for $199.95.
curiosity.detail: Levitan’s April column describes a built-in 300-bps modem, speakerphone and 24-button automatic dialer storing up to 30 digits per number; busy-number auto-redial is also described. RS-232-equipped computers can use the new Panasonic models. This is a CES product report, not proof of an April launch.

gadgetWatch.headline: Panasonic combines speakerphone and 300-bps modem
gadgetWatch.summary: KX-D4130 phone/modem at $199.95, reported in April COMPUTE! after Winter CES; 24-button dialer and handsfree speakerphone. Consumer-telephone crossover, not an exact-week announcement.
